query: Consider the following context: Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. In that context, which method can be used for overcome the strength-ductility trade-off, and why?

generation.hypothesis: The strength-ductility trade-off in conventional materials can be overcome by designing high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with specific microstructures and compositions that simultaneously achieve high strength, high ductility, and good oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy (HEA) with a composition of AlCoCrFeNi
generation.intervention: Stationary friction processing (SFP) to refine the grain size and create an ultrafine-grain microstructure
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 h
generation.structural_mediator: Ultrafine-grain microstructure with high grain boundary density
generation.mechanism: The ultrafine-grain microstructure facilitates rapid outward diffusion of Cr ions to form a dense, protective Cr₂O₃ layer, followed by the formation of Al-rich inner oxides via inward oxygen diffusion, resulting in enhanced oxidation resistance and improved mechanical properties
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved strength, ductility, and oxidation resistance of the HEA
generation.baseline: As-cast HEA with a coarse grain size
generation.boundary: The ultrafine-grain microstructure is stable up to 1050 °C
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of the phase transformation from BCC/B2 to FCC during SFP is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the mechanical properties and oxidation resistance of as-cast and SFP-processed HEAs
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SFP-processed HEA does not show improved strength, ductility, and oxidation resistance compared to the as-cast HEA, the hypothesis is falsified

Question: How can high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be designed to simultaneously achieve high fracture strength and high ductility while overcoming issues of inferior castability and compositional segregation?. System: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA). Processing: Vacuum induction melting of commercially pure elements (Al, Co, Ni: 99.9 wt.%; Cr, Fe: 99.5 ~ 99.6 wt.%) in a BN crucible; heating to 600°C for 1 hour; pouring at 1500°C into a MgO crucible (220 mm length, 62 mm upper ID, 50 mm bottom ID) under argon atmosphere (0.06 MPa); subsequent cold rolling with 8% thickness reduction for some specimens.. Paper card. Question: How does an ultrafine-grain microstructure, obtained via stationary friction processing, affect the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: Equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Stationary friction processing (SFP) using a WC-cylindrical tool (12 mm diameter) at rotational speeds of 400 rpm and 1800 rpm for 5 min duration. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 h. Findings: Grain size refined from 98 μm (as-cast) to 1 μm (SFP_400) and 0.43 μm (SFP_1800).; Phase transformation from BCC/B2 to FCC occurred, with 38% and 55% FCC fraction for SFP_400 and SFP_1800, respectively.; Surface free energy increased by 29.8% for SFP_400 and 35.2% for SFP_1800 compared to as-cast.; Oxidation kinetics decelerated by 12–20% for SFP_400 and 38–48% for SFP_1800 compared to as-cast.; Cumulative mass gain at 850 °C after 100 h was 0.33 mg/cm² (as-cast), 0.27 mg/cm² (SFP_400), and 0.17 mg/cm² (SFP_1800).; Parabolic rate constants (k_p) at 1050 °C were 23.2 × 10⁻¹³ g²·cm⁻⁴·s⁻¹ (as-cast), 18.4 × 10⁻¹³ (SFP_400), and 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ (SFP_1800).; Processed samples formed predominantly protective
